new_statements.quote: [p.175, sec.1.1] ラワ語における "音韻的な語" (phonological word), すなわち, 強勢や音調を考えなければその連続が "音韻論的に文法的な文" となるような最小の音韻形式は, 原則として次のような型で構成されている。(1) (C4V4)C1(C2)V1(V2)(V3)(C3) […] C4V4 を副音節 (minor syllable), 残りを主音節 (major syllable) […] と, それぞれ, 呼ぶことにする。 [p.179, sec.1.4] 各音素の音価は一般に主音節における場合と同じであって, ただ, 母音が常に弱くかつ短いという点だけが異なっている。特に a の音価は特定の環境で鼻音化・口蓋化されることもなく常に弱短母音であって, (ə と誤解される恐れのない限り) [ə] で表わす。
new_statements.translation: [p.175, sec.1.1] The 'phonological word' in Lawa, that is, the minimal phonological form such that, if stress and intonation are left out of account, a sequence of them forms a 'phonologically grammatical sentence', is in principle built on the following pattern: (1) (C4V4)C1(C2)V1(V2)(V3)(C3) […] We shall call C4V4 the minor syllable and the remainder the major syllable […]. [p.179, sec.1.4] The phonetic value of each phoneme [in the minor syllable] is in general the same as in the major syllable; the only difference is that the vowel is always weak and short. In particular the value of a is never nasalized or palatalized in particular environments but is always a weak short vowel, and is written [ə] (as long as there is no risk of confusing it with ə).
new_statements.citation: Mitani, Yasuyuki. 1972. Studies in the Lawa Phonology [in Japanese]. Tōnan Ajia Kenkyū 10(2):174-196.
new_statements.locator: p.175 sec. 1.1 音節の構成 (PDF p.2) and p.179 sec. 1.4 副音節 (PDF p.6); English abstract p.174 (PDF p.1)
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed: final syllable (major-syllable) coding from Ratanakul & Ratanahongse 1985 and adds the explicit word template (one optional weak minor syllable + word-final major syllable, so words are at most sesquisyllabic) and the phonetic characterization of the minor-syllable vowel as always weak and short, across three dialects. It does not itself state where stress falls, so it cannot be a deciding source for placement; the catalog's Ratanakul & Ratanahongse 1985 p.271 remains the deciding statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mitani never states a stress rule; he explicitly sets stress and intonation aside when defining the phonological word (p.175). What he does give is the word template: at most one minor syllable (C4V4, V4 limited to a, i, u) followed by one major syllable, i.e. a sesquisyllable whose full syllable is word-final, and the statement that the minor-syllable vowel is always weak and short (p.179, [ə]). That is compatible with, and implicitly supports, the catalog's final/major-syllable stress (final stress), but it is an inference from the weak/short minor syllable, not a placement statement. Chapter II (pp.180-196, generative phonology) discusses only segmental redundancy; the one other prosodic mention (p.180) excludes 'sentence intonation' from the formative's phonetic representation.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress. Notes that most minor syllables are prefixes or grammatical morphemes (B. pi-, ka-, ma-, ʔi-; U., M. pa-, ka-) and that only a very few lexical items have a minor syllable of their own (e.g. B. ku-, U. la-); a /·/ boundary is written when a CV sequence could be read as either a major or a minor syllable (p.179).
new_statements.identity_note: Mitani 1972 describes three dialects: Bo Luang (B), Umphai (U) and Mae Sariang (M). Bo Luang is Eastern Lawa (Glottolog east2330, ISO lwl), while Umphai and Mae Sariang belong to Western Lawa (west2396), the catalog's languoid; the catalog's deciding source (Ratanakul & Ratanahongse 1985) is the Ban Pa Pae variety in Mae Sariang district, also Western Lawa. The quoted statements (word template, weak short minor-syllable vowel) are given for all three dialects without distinction.

(2) Deciding source is a 46-page dedicated phonology article (1985) on exactly this languoid's dialect (Ban Pa Pae, Mae Sariang = Western Lawa), with an explicit Stress Group statement: nucleus stressed, always final; periphery weakly stressed (minor syllable, open or closed) or unstressed (CV presyllable, /i ə u/ only); trisyllables only Thai loans, also final-stressed. Glottolog lists no fuller grammar or later phonology for west2396; the one grammar sketch (Jiranan 1985, held) agrees on p.19. sources.quote: 'When morphemes are not monosyllabic the initial syllable is made up of an unstressed minor syllable which is almost always /sə pə kə rə lə/ except in borrowed words ... Trisyllabic words are very rare, and are usually compounds.' Also p.279: 'In two syllable words the vowel of the minor syllable /ə/ is predictable, and not written.'
sources.note: Primary source behind the held Jiranan 1985 phonology summary (La-Up dialect); states initial minor syllable is unstressed (p.278) — corroborates final stress from an independent fieldworker.

sources.quote: Sec. 1.1 defines the phonological word 'setting aside stress and tone' as (C V)(minor syllable) + main syllable; sec. 1.4: the phonemes of the minor syllable have the same values as in the main syllable 'except that the vowel is always weak and short' (母音が常に弱くかつ短い), written [ə]. No explicit stress-placement rule, but the sesquisyllabic (minor + major-final) structure matches the coding.
